Subject: VPC egress TLS signer & legacy-host mapping for private endpoints

Hi Irene,

Thanks for taking this — ACME is preparing a private deployment with Redwood (staging VPC first, then prod). Two items we need to lock down before we hand off to procurement:

1) TLS signer model: we have some legacy hostnames (internal-only FQDNs that clients still hit) and a set of new canonical FQDNs we'd like Redwood to present. We *prefer* to supply our own certs (BYOC), but if Redwood can provision short-lived certs tied to our private CA (or a managed CA contract) that would be helpful — we just need clear rotation and OCSP/CRL behavior.

2) Hostname mapping / DNS: our environment uses split-horizon DNS. The customer-facing canonical hostnames need to resolve to the Redwood private endpoint inside our VPC; legacy hostnames must continue to work for some older clients that do not SNI correctly. How does Redwood recommend handling SNI fallback / SNI-to-hostheader mapping and the shadow DNS we keep internally?

Attached is a one-page summary of our cert requirements and the list of legacy hostnames. Can you confirm recommended workflow and next steps? Also: any necessary procurement artifacts (e.g., cert signing templates or compliance attestations) would help us move faster.

Hi Samira — appreciate the summary. Short answers up front, detailed options below:

TL;DR: We support both BYOC (customer uploads cert + private key / or CSR + signed cert) and Redwood-managed certs (short-lived, automated rotation). For legacy-hostname compatibility we typically run an SNI mapping table on the edge and keep a separate internal DNS shadow to map legacy names to the same backend; where SNI is absent we fall back to host-header mapping.

Options and tradeoffs:
- BYOC via CSR: Customer generates a CSR (we can provide examples) and uploads the signed cert + intermediate chain. Redwood will handle installation and rotation windows, but the customer owns key material and must coordinate renewals. Pros: customer retains private key control; cons: manual rotations unless automated by the customer's issuance pipeline.
- Redwood-managed short-lived certs: We can provision certs on your behalf using an internal PKI or ACME flow bound to the private FQDNs. We automate rotation every N days (configurable), publish OCSP stapling where relevant, and can provide logs for audit. Pros: lower ops burden; cons: requires trust agreement and KMS access patterns we document.

DNS / SNI mapping notes:
- For split-horizon DNS, you should continue to own the internal zone. We will accept the internal record pointing at the private endpoint IP(s).
- SNI fallback: if clients do not send SNI, we map based on the Host header. For truly legacy clients that also lack a valid host header, we need one canonical legacy name configured as a fallback on the proxy.
- We strongly recommend adding SANs for both legacy and canonical names in the certs (including internal SRV if you use service discovery).

Next steps I propose:
1) Confirm whether you want BYOC or Redwood-managed certs.
2) If BYOC: send the CSR (we attached an example CSR template). If Redwood-managed: fill out the short PKI consent form (we will send link).
3) Tech call to validate split-horizon records and SNI behavior — can you do Thu 10am PT?

Sharing an example CSR and a short runbook for mapping in the staging VPC.

Thanks,
Irene Choi
Senior Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Karthik / team —

Quick update (results attached):
- BYOC install flow: validated with a staging RSA4096 cert, SANs included for both legacy.internal.acme and api.acme.private. Install and reload succeed without proxy downtime.
- SNI fallback: SNI+host header and no-SNI+host header both route correctly. For the no-SNI+no-host header legacy clients we were able to match fallback name and successful backend routing, but only if the legacy name is present as a configured fallback on the proxy (we used legacy.internal.acme).
- OCSP: stapling works for staging issuer; when stapling absent the proxy falls back to cached CRL (configurable TTL).

Recommendations:
1) ACME should include legacy.internal.acme as a SAN on the cert to avoid fallback edge cases.
2) Use SHA256 with RSA4096 for prod certs per their compliance request (note: this increases cert size and TLS handshake slightly).
3) Documented DNS needs: split-horizon A records pointing legacy and canonical names to the same private endpoint IPs; also add an internal PTR record for troubleshooting.

Files uploaded: test-results-20280511.txt and a short runbook. I created the JIRA INF-3127 and linked the Drive folder: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1ACME-Certs
